Circles And Square

GeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two circles drawn on a square always meet a second time on the same diagonal.
How to play: Drag the points A, B, C, D, M, N and K, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick Names for labels or press Reset diagram to start over.
Look for the math

Drag the points and the two circles change shape. Their second meeting point moves too — but it never leaves the diagonal of the square. Why not?

The picture

Start with square ABCD. Choose M on side AD, N on side BC, and any point K on the line MN. Draw the circumcircle of triangle AMK and the circumcircle of triangle CNK. Besides K, the circles meet once more at P. The page claims P always lies on the diagonal AC, and the logic test confirms it for more than six hundred drawings: the signed area of triangle ACP is zero every time.

Why the two angles add up

When the four points A, M, K, P form a convex cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles add to 180°, so ∠APK + ∠AMK = 180°. The sides AD and BC are parallel, and MK and NK are the same line seen from opposite ends, so ∠AMK = ∠KNC. Together, ∠APK + ∠KPC = 180°, which is exactly what it means for A, P and C to lie on one straight line. The test checks both angle facts: the angles at M and N agree in every drawing, and the two angles at P add to a straight angle wherever AMKP is convex.

It works beyond squares

Nowhere in that argument did we use equal side lengths — only that AD is parallel to BC. So the claim also holds for rectangles and for any parallelogram, as the page's remark says. The logic test draws slanted parallelograms too, and P lands on their diagonal AC as well.

When the circles touch

If K happens to sit where MN crosses AC, the circles have only one common point: P and K coincide on the diagonal, and the circles have a common tangent there. When the two crossings are less than a pixel apart, the applet's own rule for picking the point beside K can choose K itself; the test leaves those few near-touching drawings to the tangent check rather than claiming a visible second point.

Try this: drag M and N far apart, then slide K slowly along MN and watch P stay on the diagonal.
